li.a: Vice: Murder, Extortion, and Gelato: a History of the Calabrian Mafia in Australia
Sydney Crime Museum: The Woodward Royal Commission
The Canberra Times: AFP's Nigel Ryan says Operation Ironside revealed impact of Calabrian mafia 'Ndrangheta in Australia
Policing Insight: A flurry of attention, then collective forgetfulness
The Sydney Morning Herald: Married to the mob
BBC News: Mafia 'linked to senior Australian politicians'
The Sydney Morning Herald: Australian alleged mafia figures named in Italian court

content.p: The Honoured Society is the name given in Australia to the Calabrian 'Ndrangheta, the southern Italian criminal network that the BBC calls one of the world's most powerful criminal groups. Writers date its Australian history to 1922. Its public profile has risen and fallen ever since: a burst of attention after the disappearance of a Griffith anti-drug campaigner in 1977, another after a 2015 media investigation into political donations, and a third in 2022 when the Australian Federal Police said it had identified 14 'Ndrangheta-affiliated clans.

The record is uneven. Some of what is known comes from court findings and convictions. Much comes from leaked police reports, journalism, inquests and Italian court papers, in which named people are alleged or suspected members, not convicted ones. This account marks that line where it matters.

Accounts of the first arrivals differ. Vice says a ship called the Re d'Italia left Calabria in 1922, docked at Adelaide and put ashore three 'Ndrangheta members. Policing Insight, written by an author who says he or she has researched the Australian 'Ndrangheta since 2014, gives a date, 18 December 1922, and says the ship, which it calls the King of Italy, called at Fremantle, then Adelaide, then Melbourne, leaving one of three founders at each port.

According to Vice, the Society's first local business was fruit and vegetables, where it extorted farmers and charged market stallholders for protection, and it later moved into drugs, kidnapping and extortion. Vice also reports a war between the newly arrived Calabrians and Sicilians who had come about two decades earlier, and attributes ten murders in northern Queensland between 1928 and 1940 to that infighting.

By the 1960s, Vice writes, Calabrians held a stranglehold over Melbourne's wholesale fruit and vegetable trade. Then a market worker named Vincenzo Angilletta was shot twice through the rear window of his car in the driveway of his Northcote home. Vice says it was thought Angilletta had founded a breakaway faction called La Bastarda, which had about 300 members at its peak, and that his death was allegedly ordered by the Australian Crimine, a board that answers to headquarters in Italy. In 1964 Vincenzo Muratore, described as the Society's money man, was killed the same way.

The killings drew in outside investigators. Vice names John T. Cusack of the US Bureau of Narcotics and the Calabrian assistant police commissioner Ugo Macera as the men sent to examine the group, and says neither report has been made public. Leaked extracts of Cusack's findings, quoted by Vice, described a Calabrian society "well entrenched in Australia" and already involved in extortion, prostitution, counterfeiting, illegal gambling and the smuggling of people and small arms. Policing Insight adds that Australian institutions recognised the particular character of the 'Ndrangheta between the mid-1950s and mid-1960s, sooner than Italian authorities, who were then focused on the Sicilian Cosa Nostra.

In July 1977 Donald Mackay, a Liberal Party anti-drug campaigner, vanished from the car park of the Griffith Hotel in the New South Wales Riverina after drinks with friends. Vice reports bloodstains on his locked van and three .22 shell casings on the bitumen. It says his name had been leaked as the whistleblower during a trial of four Calabrian men who had grown a large marijuana crop at Coleambally, about 40 miles south of Griffith. Vice says Robert Trimboli, a Griffith man who owned a yacht called Cannabis, was charged over the murder and fled to Spain. A 2002 Sydney Morning Herald feature calls "Aussie Bob" Trimbole a principal of the Mr Asia cartel and names him among Griffith powerbrokers it says ordered Mackay's death, and says James Bazley was paid to kill him.

The Sydney Crime Museum's account of the aftermath shows how quickly politics followed. Premier Wran told reporters on 9 July that he would form a drugs royal commission, and four days later offered a $25,000 reward. Prime Minister Fraser then set up a Commonwealth royal commission, and, according to the museum, Wran then announced a state inquiry under Mr Justice Woodward. Its first hearing was on 10 August 1977, three weeks after Mackay disappeared. The Australian newspaper ran a story headed "Griffith - In the Bloody Grip of the Mafia".
content.h2: What the Royal Commission did and did not prove
content.p: The commission moved to Griffith in early September and, the museum's account says, became fixated on solving the Mackay case. Counsel assisting, William Fisher, QC, used what the museum calls a paper-chase method, adding up the assets of suspected growers to show they had more than farming could explain. Francesco Barbaro, who owned a nine-hectare farm and was married to Antonio Sergi's sister, averaged a net annual income of $399 between 1969 and 1972, then built a $190,000 house shell in 1975. Sergi's assets totalled $2,649,792 and those of his partner Robert Trimboli exceeded $3 million. The commission also found that Detective Sergeant John Ellis, whose sympathetic evidence helped cut the four cultivators' sentences from jail to fines in 1974, had about $55,000 in assets beyond his income.

After nine months Fisher told the hearings that the structure of the cultivation was consistent with the origins of the Honoured Society and pointed to what he called a secretive organisation which "probably" had links over most of Australia. The Council for Civil Liberties called this a "slur on the Italian community" without basis in the evidence. The final report, released in November 1979, concluded that the eastern Australian marijuana trade was controlled by a highly organised Calabrian group based in Griffith and linked to the secret society, and that it was "probably" responsible for Mackay's murder, according to the museum's summary.

That account is itself a critique. Its author argues that the commission never confirmed a nationwide Calabrian mafia, that the report said nothing about who moved the cannabis once it reached Sydney, and that the commission's use of the word "Mafia", like the press's and Mackay's widow's, rested more on ethnic stereotype than hard evidence. Tensions in Griffith were real: the museum says Italians stayed at home for several days after Mackay vanished, fearing retaliation. The two readings, a Calabrian secret society on one side and a small farming network at the bottom of a longer distribution chain on the other, have run side by side since.
content.h2: Canberra, Operation Seville and the Winchester inquest
content.p: The Canberra Times connects the group to another unsolved question. Colin Winchester, an assistant commissioner of the Australian Federal Police, was shot in a Deakin driveway in January 1989. David Eastman was charged with the murder and served 19 years in jail; he was acquitted in 2014 and was paid more than $7 million in compensation. The paper reports that evidence at the 1990 inquest showed Winchester had been a key figure in Operation Seville, which sought to identify leading figures of the 'Ndrangheta, also called the Honoured Society.

In the early 1980s, the paper says, eleven Italian men, known as the Bungendore 11, were under surveillance and due to face court, but all charges were dropped after a key informant failed to testify. Two large cannabis crops grown in the Tallaganda State Forest were the focus; at least part of the harvest was taken without police knowledge and millions of dollars went missing. The inquest also heard of documents seized from one man's home that set out an initiation rite in which members cut their thumbs in the shape of a cross.
content.h2: Murder, informers and extortion in the 1980s
content.p: Vice describes the decade as one of growing profit and growing violence. It cites researcher Anna Sergi's judgment that "New South Wales has been turned into a huge mafia corporation" and an estimate that cannabis earned about $60 million a year. In 1982 Domenic Marafiote disappeared after passing the names of Society members and the locations of plantations to police; his parents were also shot dead at their Adelaide home, and his body was found five years later in a shallow grave in a chicken coop in Victoria.

The group's demands reached the supermarkets, Vice says. It reports that Coles estimated it was paying $6 million a year in the early 1980s, a charge of 50 cents on each box of produce. A Coles employee who had asked about the extra fees, John Vassilopoulos, was shot with a shotgun when he opened his door at his Ivanhoe home; he survived, and the company relocated him and six colleagues. Geelong Football Club president Frank Costa, whom Coles asked to take over its produce supply, was offered $1 million a year to leave the Society alone and was threatened with death when he refused, Vice reports. During the Melbourne gangland war that began in 1998 with the killing of Alphonse Gangitano, the Society stayed on the margins, with one major loss: the boss Frank Benvenuto, shot in the driveway of his Beaumaris home in 2000.
content.h2: The Griffith sting and a killing in an orchard
content.p: The Sydney Morning Herald's 2002 feature tells how a Victorian detective, using the alias Cole Goodwin, posed as an art dealer in 1993 and befriended Tony Romeo and Rosario Trimbole, nephew of "Aussie Bob" Trimbole. The two men, then in their late 30s, were treated by the paper as peers in the Society's pecking order. Over months they dined with the undercover officers in Melbourne and let slip plans. In early 1994 they agreed to help import $6 million of cannabis from Papua New Guinea. They were arrested on 19 June 1994, five followers with them, and the paper says the evidence was so damning that Romeo and Trimbole pleaded guilty and received 13 years with a minimum of eight.

Romeo was released and returned to Griffith despite warnings. Six weeks later, on 1 July, he was shot dead while pruning a peach tree, with about 30 people working nearby, none of whom saw anything. A Toyota stolen from the town six weeks earlier was found burned out about 50 kilometres away the same day. The paper, which suggested he may have wronged his wife and so the Society's code, called the killing a puzzle and noted police had a poor record with such crimes.
content.h2: Politics, money and Italian court papers
content.p: A joint investigation by Fairfax Media and the ABC's Four Corners, reported by BBC News in June 2015, said politicians of both major parties had been lobbied by donors linked to the group. It quoted a 2013 police report saying the 'Ndrangheta had used well-known donors to give itself a "legitimate public face". The report said a man with "deep mafia associations" met then Prime Minister John Howard at a Liberal Party fundraiser in the early 2000s, with no suggestion that Howard knew of any criminal links.

Vice recounts one lobbying campaign. In 2005 the Melbourne lawyer Joseph Acquaro helped secure a visa for Francesco Madafferi, who had overstayed a tourist visa for 12 years; then immigration minister Amanda Vanstone allowed him to stay on humanitarian grounds. Three years later Madafferi was arrested in a seizure of 15 million ecstasy pills hidden in tomato tins, along with 17 others. In March 2016 Acquaro was shot dead behind his Lygon Street gelato shop. Vice says early reports suggested he may have leaked information to journalists, and that a court in December 2015 found it reasonable for police to suspect Antonio Madafferi had put out a $200,000 contract on a man he believed was an informant to The Age. Those are suspicions; no conviction is reported in the pages cited.

In February 2020 The Age and the Sydney Morning Herald reported that Italian court papers from Operation Eyphemos named two Melbourne produce businessmen, Tony Madafferi and Diego Luppino, as alleged local bosses. The paper stressed that neither man was accused of a crime in Italy or Australia, and that both vehemently denied the claims. Luppino's son called them baseless.
content.h2: Operation Ironside and the long view
content.p: On 8 June 2021 the AFP and FBI carried out the overt phase of Operation Ironside, which used an encrypted phone network. A year later Assistant Commissioner Nigel Ryan said police had identified 51 Italian organised crime clans in Australia, 14 of them confirmed as 'Ndrangheta-affiliated, with thousands of members. He said the group used legitimate construction, agriculture and catering businesses as fronts, and was "pulling the strings" of some outlaw motorcycle gangs. Policing Insight, quoting the AFP, reports that 383 alleged offenders have been charged in Australia over Ironside, with 2,340 offences.

The same Policing Insight author argues the 2022 statements were not news to someone who had studied the group for a decade, and that Australian policy swings between "a flurry of attention" and "collective forgetfulness". The author also points to political infiltration and legitimate businesses built on crime proceeds as less discussed than drugs.
